blogs.title: Updating “Ongoing”: What Farahi v. FBI Says About Staleness and FOIA Exemption 7(A)
blogs.description: This post would examine the D.C. Circuit’s treatment of time-sensitive Exemption 7(A) claims, focusing on the district court’s insistence on updated declarations and the panel’s acceptance of a terse supplemental declaration when read against earlier, more detailed submissions. It would analyze how Farahi fits with CREW and Juarez on what counts as a “pending or reasonably anticipated” enforcement proceeding, and what agencies must do when years pass during FOIA litigation.

blogs.title: Deference, National Security, and the FBI File: Farahi’s Reinforcement of FOIA Exceptionalism
blogs.description: This post would explore the opinion’s strong reliance on deference to the FBI as a law-enforcement agency, especially where counterterrorism and national security concerns are implicated. It would discuss how the court layers ordinary Exemption 7 deference with the heightened solicitude seen in cases like CNSS, and consider whether Farahi signals a broader trend toward permitting relatively generalized public justifications when sealed submissions fill in the details.

blogs.title: How Much Can Be Hidden in Secret? Ex Parte Declarations and Segregability After Farahi
blogs.description: This post would focus on the court’s approval of the district court’s reliance on sealed, ex parte declarations both to sustain Exemption 7(A) and to reject segregability. It would analyze the tension between FOIA’s transparency mission and the practical necessity of secret judicial review, especially where the court concludes that only isolated words or phrases could be released. The post would also consider the procedural significance of Farahi’s failure to object to ex parte submissions and what that means for future FOIA litigants.

blogs.title: Category-by-Category Withholding and the Cost of Underdeveloped Appellate Arguments
blogs.description: This post would look at the panel’s brief but important treatment of categorical withholding and forfeiture. The court reaffirmed that agencies must define categories with enough specificity to test exemption claims, yet it refused to engage because Farahi did not concretely explain why the FBI’s categories were overbroad. The post would use this aspect of the case to discuss how FOIA doctrine increasingly turns not only on substantive exemption law, but on careful issue preservation and targeted challenges to agency Vaughn-style presentations.
